faq.lostQ: What is lost when converting {F} to {T}?
faq.lostA: {T} keeps: {keeps}. Anything {F} stores beyond that is dropped.
mesh: Why is my model the wrong size?

Formats store units differently: STL has none, glTF uses metres, 3MF and STEP record units. If the result looks 1000 times too small or large, pick a different option in Scale (for example “Metres → mm”) and convert again.
Why is my model lying on its side?
Some formats treat Y as up (glTF, OBJ, FBX), others Z (STL, 3MF, STEP). “Up axis: Automatic” rotates the model for the target format. Choose “Keep as is” if you prefer the original orientation.
faq.imageBestLitho: Use a well-lit photo with clear contrast. Crop it to the shape you want before uploading. Faces and landscapes work well; very dark photos come out thick and dim.
faq.imageBestOther: For logos and text use a high-contrast PNG (black shapes on white or transparent). For reliefs, any photo works, but simple images with strong light and dark areas give the clearest result.
image: What settings should I print a lithophane with?
Lithophanes are usually printed upright in white PLA with 100% infill and fine layers (0.12–0.16 mm) so the thickness differences show clearly. Check your slicer’s recommendations for your printer.
Can I change the size later?
Yes. Set the width here, or scale the STL in your slicer. Scaling in the slicer also scales the thickness, so set the thickness here for the best control.
svg: Why are some parts of my SVG missing?

Only filled shapes and stroked lines are turned into 3D. Text must be converted to paths first (in Inkscape: Path → Object to Path; in Illustrator: Type → Create Outlines). Embedded bitmaps are ignored.
How do I make a cookie cutter or keychain?
Use a simple outline. Extrude it with a small thickness for a keychain, or combine a thin tall wall and a wider base in your slicer or CAD app for a cutter.
dds: Which DDS compression should I choose?
DXT5 (BC3) keeps smooth transparency and suits most game textures. DXT1 (BC1) gives the smallest files but only on/off transparency. Uncompressed RGBA is exact but four to eight times larger.
Most games expect mipmaps for textures shown at different distances; they reduce shimmering. UI images and icons usually do not need them.
Which DDS files can be opened?
DXT1, DXT3, DXT5 and uncompressed DDS files. BC7 files that use the newer DX10 header are not supported yet.
viewer: Which formats can the viewer open?
STL, 3MF, OBJ, GLB, glTF, FBX, PLY, DAE, 3DS, USDZ, OFF, AMF, VRML (WRL), STEP, STP, IGES, IGS and G-code, plus ZIP archives that contain a model.

Dimensions come straight from the file’s coordinates and are shown in the file’s own units (millimetres for most 3D-printing files). Volume is exact for closed (watertight) meshes; for open meshes it is only an estimate.
Files with a few million triangles open on most computers. Very large scans may be slow on phones because everything runs on your device.

3mf-stl: Most 3MF files you meet are slicer projects from Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, PrusaSlicer or MakerWorld. Each object on the plate is kept; merge them into one STL or download one STL per object.
Print settings, painted supports, colour painting and plate layout live only in the 3MF project. STL keeps the shape, so re-apply those settings in your slicer after importing.
stl-3mf: 3MF stores units, so a model converted here is tagged as millimetres and opens at the right size in Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer and Cura.
A 3MF file is a compressed ZIP, so it is usually smaller than the same binary STL.
glb-stl: GLB is the usual download from AI 3D generators (Meshy, Tripo, Rodin and others) and from web viewers. Converting to STL keeps the shape and drops colours and textures, which slicers cannot use anyway.
glTF uses metres and Y-up. We rotate the model so it stands upright in your slicer; if it looks tiny, choose “Metres → mm” in Scale.
AI-generated meshes are often open or self-intersecting. Check the model in your slicer and use its repair option before printing.
step-stl: STEP stores exact CAD surfaces. To make an STL, curved faces are split into triangles (tessellation). We use a fine setting so holes and fillets stay smooth.
Assemblies keep every part. Download one STL for the whole assembly or one per part.
stp-stl: .stp and .step are the same format, so this works exactly like STEP to STL: exact CAD surfaces are tessellated into a fine triangle mesh.
obj-stl: OBJ files from Blender, ZBrush or 3D scanners often come with textures. STL keeps only the geometry, which is what a slicer needs.
OBJ is usually Y-up. We rotate the model to Z-up so it lies correctly on the build plate.
stl-obj: Use OBJ to bring a print model into Blender, Maya or a game engine. STL has no units, so check the scale after importing (Blender treats 1 unit as 1 metre).
fbx-obj: FBX is common for game assets and Mixamo characters. OBJ keeps the mesh and UVs; skeletons and animation are not part of OBJ, so the model is exported in its current pose.
fbx-stl: Rigged characters are exported in the pose stored in the file. Thin parts such as hair cards or flat clothing may need thickening before they will print.
glb-obj: Useful when a tool accepts OBJ but not glTF. Geometry and UVs are kept; PBR materials are simplified.
gcode-stl: G-code contains printer moves, not the model you sliced. We rebuild a solid from each extruded line using the detected layer height and a 0.45 mm line width, so you get a close approximation for previews and measurements.
If you still have the original STL or 3MF, use that instead: it will be far cleaner.
zip-stl: Model sites often deliver STL files inside ZIP archives. We open the archive in your browser and convert the first model inside. If the ZIP holds several models, you will see which one was used.
ply-stl: PLY files from 3D scanners can be point clouds. Only PLY files with faces (triangles) can be converted to a printable STL.
stl-dxf: The mesh is written as 3DFACE entities, which AutoCAD, LibreCAD and most CAM programs can open. DXF from a mesh is not a 2D drawing; for laser cutting you still need a flat outline.

stl.what: STL is the most common file for 3D printing. It stores a surface as a list of triangles and nothing else: no colours, no materials, no units. Every slicer can open it.
stl.usedBy: Every slicer (Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer, Cura), Thingiverse and Printables downloads, most CAD tools as an export.
stl.keeps: Triangle geometry only. Binary STL is about five times smaller than ASCII STL.
stl.notes: STL has no unit field. Slicers assume millimetres, so a model exported in metres or inches can appear tiny or huge.

3mf.what: 3MF is a ZIP-based format designed to replace STL. It stores the mesh with units, colours, several objects and, in slicer projects, plate and print settings.
3mf.usedBy: Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer, Cura, Windows 3D Builder; MakerWorld and Printables project files.
3mf.keeps: Meshes, units (usually millimetres), object names, colours and materials, build-plate layout; slicer projects add their own settings.
3mf.notes: Slicer-specific data such as Bambu Studio plate settings or painted supports is not part of the core standard, so it is dropped when converting to other formats.

obj.what: OBJ is a plain-text 3D format supported almost everywhere. It stores vertices, faces and texture coordinates; materials live in a separate .mtl file.
obj.usedBy: Blender, Maya, 3ds Max, ZBrush, game engines, photogrammetry and 3D-scanning apps.
obj.keeps: Geometry, UV coordinates, normals, groups. Colours and textures only through the companion .mtl and image files.

glb.what: GLB is the single-file, binary form of glTF, the standard for 3D on the web, in AR and in many AI 3D generators. Geometry, materials and textures are packed into one file.
glb.usedBy: Web viewers, three.js, Babylon.js, Blender, AR on Android, AI model generators such as Meshy, Tripo and Rodin.
glb.keeps: Meshes, PBR materials, textures, scene hierarchy, animation. Units are metres and Y is up.
glb.notes: For 3D printing only the shape matters, so materials and textures are dropped when you convert GLB to STL.

gltf.what: glTF is the JSON version of the web 3D standard. The .gltf file may reference separate .bin and texture files, or embed them.
gltf.usedBy: Web and game engines, Blender, Sketchfab, AR tools.
gltf.keeps: Same content as GLB: meshes, materials, textures, animation.
gltf.notes: If your .gltf comes with .bin or image files, add them together so nothing is missing.

fbx.what: FBX is Autodesk’s interchange format for animation and games. It can hold meshes, skeletons, animation and materials.
fbx.usedBy: Maya, 3ds Max, Unity, Unreal Engine, Mixamo, Blender.
fbx.notes: FBX is a closed format. We read it in the browser; writing FBX needs Autodesk’s SDK, so FBX export is not offered.

ply.what: PLY was created for 3D scanning. It stores triangles and, often, a colour per vertex.
ply.keeps: Vertices, faces, vertex colours and normals. Some PLY files are point clouds without faces.

dae.what: DAE (COLLADA) is an older XML interchange format still exported by SketchUp and some game tools.
dae.usedBy: SketchUp, Google Earth models, older game pipelines.

3ds.what: 3DS is the legacy 3D Studio format. It is still found in old model libraries.

usdz.what: USDZ is Apple’s AR format, based on Pixar’s USD. iPhones and iPads open it directly in AR Quick Look.
usdz.usedBy: iOS and macOS AR Quick Look, Reality Composer, object-capture apps.
usdz.notes: Complex USD features (variants, layers) are not read by browser loaders; simple USDZ models work best.

off.what: OFF is a simple text mesh format used in geometry research and some academic tools.

amf.what: AMF is an XML format for 3D printing that was largely replaced by 3MF.

wrl.what: WRL (VRML) is an early web 3D format still used by some colour 3D printers and CAD tools.
wrl.usedBy: Colour powder printers, some CAD exports.

step.what: STEP is the main neutral CAD format. Unlike STL it stores exact surfaces (B-rep), so curves stay perfectly smooth.
step.usedBy: Fusion, SolidWorks, Onshape, FreeCAD, Inventor, CATIA, manufacturers’ part libraries.
step.keeps: Exact solid geometry, assemblies, part names, colours.
step.notes: Converting STEP to a mesh is reliable. The reverse (STL to STEP) only wraps triangles in a STEP file and does not recreate smooth CAD surfaces.

stp.what: .stp is simply another extension for a STEP file. The content is identical to .step.

iges.what: IGES is an older neutral CAD format, often used for surfaces in automotive and aerospace work.
iges.usedBy: Legacy CAD systems, CNC and CAM tools.

igs.what: .igs is the short extension for IGES files.

gcode.what: G-code is the list of machine moves a slicer sends to the printer: where to move, how fast, how much plastic to push.
gcode.usedBy: All FDM printers; produced by slicers.
gcode.keeps: Toolpaths, temperatures, speeds. Not the original model.
gcode.notes: A mesh rebuilt from G-code follows the printed lines, so it is an approximation of the original part.

dxf.what: DXF is AutoCAD’s exchange format. We export 3D meshes as 3DFACE entities that AutoCAD, LibreCAD and most CAM tools can open.
dxf.usedBy: AutoCAD, LibreCAD, laser-cutter and CNC software.

svg.what: SVG is a vector image format. Its filled shapes can be extruded into a solid for printing signs, logos, cookie cutters and stencils.
svg.usedBy: Inkscape, Illustrator, Figma, Cricut Design Space.

png.what: PNG is a lossless image format with transparency. Brightness can be turned into height to make reliefs, lithophanes and stamps.

jpg.what: JPG is the common photo format. Photos work well for lithophanes; logos are cleaner as PNG or SVG.

jpeg.what: JPEG and JPG are the same format with a different extension.

dds.what: DDS is a texture format used by games. It stores GPU-compressed images (DXT/BC) and mipmaps so textures load fast.
dds.usedBy: Game engines, modding tools for Skyrim, Fallout, Minecraft Bedrock, flight simulators.
dds.keeps: Compressed pixels, mipmaps, sometimes cube maps.
dds.notes: We read DXT1, DXT3, DXT5 and uncompressed DDS. BC7 files (DX10 header) are not supported yet.

zip.what: Many model sites ship STL files inside a ZIP. We open the archive in your browser and use the model inside.
